section: Geometrical powers of increase
label: Overproduction makes a struggle for existence inevitable
claim: Because all organisms tend to increase at a high (geometrical) rate, more individuals are produced than can survive, so every species must undergo a struggle for existence with members of its own species, with other species, or with physical conditions.
quote: A struggle for existence inevitably follows from the high rate at which all organic beings tend to increase.
scope: all plants and animals in a state of nature
measurable_quantities: intrinsic rate of increase
fecundity
proportion of offspring surviving to reproduce
population growth rate over time
candidate_data: Demographic life-table databases such as COMPADRE and COMADRE, AnAge life-history data, and long-term population time series such as the Global Population Dynamics Database.

section: Rapid increase of naturalised animals and plants
label: Geometrical increase explains rapid spread of naturalised species
claim: The extraordinarily rapid increase and wide spread of introduced (naturalised) animals and plants in new countries is explained by geometrical increase under favourable conditions with reduced mortality, not by any rise in their fertility.
quote: In such cases the geometrical ratio of increase, the result of which never fails to be surprising, simply explains the extraordinarily rapid increase and wide diffusion of naturalised productions in their new homes.
scope: introduced and feral animals and plants
measurable_quantities: population growth rate of introduced species after arrival
range expansion rate
fecundity in native versus introduced range
juvenile survival in native versus introduced range
candidate_data: Naturalised-flora and invasion databases (GloNAF, GBIF occurrence time series) combined with native-versus-introduced range demographic comparisons in the published literature.

section: Geometrical powers of increase
label: Average abundance depends only indirectly on fecundity
claim: The average number of individuals of an animal or plant species depends only indirectly on how many eggs or seeds it produces; high fecundity mainly compensates for heavy destruction, usually early in life.
quote: So that in all cases, the average number of any animal or plant depends only indirectly on the number of its eggs or seeds.
scope: all animals and plants
measurable_quantities: clutch size or seed output per individual
population abundance or density
early-life mortality rate
parental care
candidate_data: Life-history trait compilations (AnAge, AVONET, TRY plant traits, FishBase) combined with abundance estimates (e.g. global bird population estimates, BioTIME, GBIF).

section: Nature of the checks to increase
label: Predation, more often than food supply, sets average numbers
claim: Although food sets the upper limit to a species' increase, very often it is destruction by predators rather than food supply that determines the species' average numbers.
quote: The amount of food for each species of course gives the extreme limit to which each can increase; but very frequently it is not the obtaining food, but the serving as prey to other animals, which determines the average numbers of a species.
scope: animal populations in nature, e.g. game birds and mammals
measurable_quantities: population density with and without predator removal
population response to food supplementation
predation mortality rate
candidate_data: Predator-removal and food-supplementation field experiments compiled in meta-analyses (data often deposited in Dryad), and long-term predator-prey time series such as the Global Population Dynamics Database.

section: Effects of climate
label: Periodic extreme cold or drought is the most effective check
claim: Climate plays an important part in determining the average numbers of a species, and periodic seasons of extreme cold or drought are the most effective of all checks on increase.
quote: Climate plays an important part in determining the average numbers of a species, and periodical seasons of extreme cold or drought, I believe to be the most effective of all checks.
scope: animal and plant populations, e.g. birds in severe winters
measurable_quantities: population change across extreme climatic events
mortality during severe winters or droughts
relative contribution of climate versus biotic factors to population fluctuations
candidate_data: Long-term bird monitoring (North American Breeding Bird Survey, Pan-European Common Bird Monitoring Scheme), BioTIME and Living Planet Index time series matched to climate records such as ERA5 or CRU.

section: Effects of climate
label: Competitors decline poleward, so climate acts more directly there
claim: The number of species, and therefore of competitors, decreases going northward, so that going north or up a mountain one more often finds stunted forms caused by the direct harmful action of climate than going south or downhill.
quote: for the number of species of all kinds, and therefore of competitors, decreases northwards; hence in going northward, or in ascending a mountain, we far oftener meet with stunted forms, due to the _directly_ injurious action of climate, than we do in proceeding southwards or in descending a mountain.
scope: plants and animals along latitudinal and elevational gradients
measurable_quantities: species richness along latitude and elevation
frequency of stunted growth forms
relative importance of abiotic versus biotic range limits
candidate_data: GBIF and BIEN occurrence data for richness gradients, sPlot vegetation plots and TRY plant height data along gradients, with climate layers such as WorldClim or CHELSA.

section: Effects of climate
label: Climate limits species mainly indirectly, by favouring competitors
claim: Climate limits species mainly indirectly, by favouring their competitors and enemies; for example, many garden plants that tolerate the local climate never become naturalised because they cannot compete with native plants or resist native animals.
quote: That climate acts in main part indirectly by favouring other species, we may clearly see in the prodigious number of plants in our gardens which can perfectly well endure our climate, but which never become naturalised, for they cannot compete with our native plants, nor resist destruction by our native animals.
scope: plants, especially cultivated exotics and native floras
measurable_quantities: fraction of cultivated exotic species that naturalise
climatic match between cultivation sites and native range
establishment success with and without competitors or herbivores
candidate_data: GloNAF naturalised-flora data compared with horticultural species lists and climate-niche data from GBIF and WorldClim, plus competitor- and herbivore-removal experiments.

section: The relation of organism to organism the most important of all relations
label: Few species reach range edges where climate alone kills them
claim: Only a few plants or animals extend their ranges so far that they are destroyed by the severity of climate alone; competition continues everywhere except at the extreme limits of life.
quote: we have reason to believe that only a few plants or animals range so far, that they are destroyed by the rigour of the climate alone.
scope: geographic range limits of plants and animals
measurable_quantities: proportion of range limits set by abiotic tolerance versus biotic interactions
performance of transplants beyond range edges with and without competitors
candidate_data: Published transplant experiments beyond range limits, together with GBIF occurrence data and physiological tolerance compilations such as GlobTherm.

section: Protection from the number of individuals
label: Many species need a large local stock to persist
claim: In many cases a large number of individuals of a species, relative to the number of its enemies, is necessary for the species to survive, which explains why rare plants can be very abundant in the few spots where they occur.
quote: On the other hand, in many cases, a large stock of individuals of the same species, relatively to the numbers of its enemies, is absolutely necessary for its preservation.
scope: plants and animals subject to predation, e.g. seed crops eaten by birds
measurable_quantities: per-capita survival or seed loss versus local population size
minimum viable population density
local abundance of rare species where present
candidate_data: Published Allee-effect and predator-satiation studies, and population time series in the Global Population Dynamics Database and COMPADRE.

section: Complex relations of all animals and plants throughout nature
label: Chains of interaction link distant species' abundances
claim: Very different organisms are linked by chains of interaction, so that the abundance of one species can determine the frequency of another through intermediate species; for example, cats may control the frequency of red clover and heartsease by way of field-mice and humble-bees.
quote: Hence it is quite credible that the presence of a feline animal in large numbers in a district might determine, through the intervention first of mice and then of bees, the frequency of certain flowers in that district!
scope: terrestrial communities of plants, pollinators, and their predators
measurable_quantities: predator density
rodent density
bumblebee nest density
seed set and abundance of bee-pollinated plants
candidate_data: Interaction-network data (GloBI, Web of Life), published trophic-cascade field studies, and bumblebee and plant monitoring data from GBIF.

section: Complex relations of all animals and plants throughout nature
label: Balanced struggles keep communities uniform over long periods
claim: Although competition between organisms constantly recurs with shifting outcomes, the opposing forces are so finely balanced that community composition stays roughly the same for long periods, even though a trifling change could tip the balance toward one organism.
quote: Battle within battle must ever be recurring with varying success; and yet in the long-run the forces are so nicely balanced, that the face of nature remains uniform for long periods of time, though assuredly the merest trifle would often give the victory to one organic being over another.
scope: natural communities of plants and animals
measurable_quantities: temporal turnover in species composition
variance in relative abundances over time
community stability metrics
candidate_data: Long-term community time series in BioTIME, the US LTER network, and pollen records from the Neotoma Paleoecology Database.

section: Struggle for life most severe between individuals and varieties of the same species; often severe between species of the same genus
label: Struggle is most severe between members of the same species
claim: The struggle for existence is almost always most severe between individuals of the same species, because they live in the same places, need the same food and face the same dangers; between varieties of a species it is nearly as severe.
quote: But the struggle almost invariably will be most severe between the individuals of the same species, for they frequent the same districts, require the same food, and are exposed to the same dangers.
scope: all organisms, including varieties of cultivated plants and domestic animals
measurable_quantities: strength of intraspecific versus interspecific competition coefficients
per-capita effects of conspecific versus heterospecific density on growth or survival
candidate_data: Meta-analyses of competition experiments and plant neighbourhood data such as ForestGEO census plots that estimate conspecific versus heterospecific density effects.

section: Struggle for life most severe between individuals and varieties of the same species; often severe between species of the same genus
label: Congeners compete more severely than species of different genera
claim: Because species of the same genus are usually similar in habits and constitution and always in structure, competition between them is generally more severe than between species of different genera.
quote: As species of the same genus have usually, though by no means invariably, some similarity in habits and constitution, and always in structure, the struggle will generally be more severe between species of the same genus, when they come into competition with each other, than between species of distinct genera.
scope: co-occurring species of plants and animals
measurable_quantities: competition strength versus phylogenetic distance
trait similarity versus relatedness
displacement of one species by a congener
candidate_data: Pairwise competition experiments related to phylogenies from Open Tree of Life or TimeTree, and co-occurrence data from sPlot or GBIF.

section: The relation of organism to organism the most important of all relations
label: Each organism's structure is shaped by its relations to other organisms
claim: The structure of every organism is related, in essential but often hidden ways, to the structure of the other organisms with which it competes, from which it must escape, or on which it preys.
quote: A corollary of the highest importance may be deduced from the foregoing remarks, namely, that the structure of every organic being is related, in the most essential yet often hidden manner, to that of all other organic beings, with which it comes into competition for food or residence, or from which it has to escape, or on which it preys.
scope: all organisms
measurable_quantities: trait variation explained by biotic versus abiotic factors
trait shifts in response to competitors, predators or prey
candidate_data: Trait databases (TRY, AVONET) combined with interaction data (GloBI) and published character-displacement studies.

section: Natural Selection: its power compared with man’s selection, its power on characters of trifling importance, its power at all ages and on both sexes
label: Natural selection preserves favourable and destroys injurious variations
claim: Because more individuals are born than can survive, individuals with any advantage, however slight, have the best chance of surviving and reproducing, while injurious variations are eliminated; this preservation of favourable and rejection of injurious variations is natural selection.
quote: This preservation of favourable variations and the rejection of injurious variations, I call Natural Selection.
scope: all organisms in nature
measurable_quantities: selection differentials and gradients on traits
heritability of traits
differential survival and reproduction
candidate_data: Compilations of selection gradients measured in wild populations, long-term field studies of wild populations, and experimental-evolution datasets such as the LTEE.

section: Natural Selection: its power compared with man’s selection, its power on characters of trifling importance, its power at all ages and on both sexes
label: Neutral variations escape selection and remain fluctuating
claim: Variations that are neither useful nor harmful are not acted on by natural selection and stay variable, which may explain the variability of so-called polymorphic species.
quote: Variations neither useful nor injurious would not be affected by natural selection, and would be left a fluctuating element, as perhaps we see in the species called polymorphic.
scope: characters of all organisms, especially polymorphic species
measurable_quantities: fitness effect of a character
variance of the character within and among populations
temporal fluctuation of character frequencies
candidate_data: Long-term studies of polymorphism frequencies in wild populations and morphological trait variance in trait databases, compared with measured selection on those traits.

section: Natural Selection: its power compared with man’s selection, its power on characters of trifling importance, its power at all ages and on both sexes
label: No native biota is so well adapted that it cannot be improved
claim: No country's native inhabitants are so perfectly adapted that none could be improved, as shown by introduced species having established firmly in every country.
quote: No country can be named in which all the native inhabitants are now so perfectly adapted to each other and to the physical conditions under which they live, that none of them could anyhow be improved; for in all countries, the natives have been so far conquered by naturalised productions, that they have allowed foreigners to take firm possession of the land.
scope: native biotas of all countries and regions
measurable_quantities: number and share of established alien species per region
displacement of native species by aliens
candidate_data: Global alien-species databases such as GloNAF, the Alien Species First Records Database, and GRIIS (Global Register of Introduced and Invasive Species).

section: Natural Selection: its power compared with man’s selection, its power on characters of trifling importance, its power at all ages and on both sexes
label: Protective colours matching backgrounds are maintained by selection
claim: Seemingly trivial characters such as colour can be shaped by natural selection; colours that match the background, as in green leaf-eating insects and heather-coloured grouse, protect their bearers from predators that hunt by sight.
quote: When we see leaf-eating insects green, and bark-feeders mottled-grey; the alpine ptarmigan white in winter, the red-grouse the colour of heather, and the black-grouse that of peaty earth, we must believe that these tints are of service to these birds and insects in preserving them from danger.
scope: animals preyed on by visually hunting predators
measurable_quantities: background matching of coloration
predation rate on matching versus mismatching morphs
coloration versus habitat across species
candidate_data: Field predation experiments on cryptic versus conspicuous prey models, comparative plumage-colour datasets from museum specimens, and long-term morph-frequency records such as those for the peppered moth.

section: Natural Selection: its power compared with man’s selection, its power on characters of trifling importance, its power at all ages and on both sexes
label: Natural selection can modify organisms at any age
claim: Because variations arising at a particular life stage tend to be inherited at the same stage, natural selection can modify organisms at any age, for instance adapting larvae independently of adults.
quote: natural selection will be enabled to act on and modify organic beings at any age, by the accumulation of profitable variations at that age, and by their inheritance at a corresponding age.
scope: all organisms, especially those with distinct life stages such as insects with larvae
measurable_quantities: selection on juvenile versus adult traits
trait correlations between life stages
stage-specific heritability
candidate_data: Studies of stage-specific selection and morphological decoupling between larvae and adults in insects and amphibians, with phylogenies from Open Tree of Life.

section: Natural Selection: its power compared with man’s selection, its power on characters of trifling importance, its power at all ages and on both sexes
label: No species has structures solely for the good of another species
claim: Natural selection cannot modify the structure of one species purely for the benefit of another species without giving it any advantage, so no such structure should be found.
quote: What natural selection cannot do, is to modify the structure of one species, without giving it any advantage, for the good of another species
scope: all species and their interspecific interactions
measurable_quantities: fitness benefit to the bearer of traits that benefit other species
costs and benefits in mutualisms
candidate_data: Studies of mutualism costs and benefits (e.g. nectar, fruit, ant-plant rewards) compiled in interaction databases such as GloBI and published meta-analyses.

section: Sexual Selection
label: Males of polygamous species fight most and carry special weapons
claim: Fighting between males for females is perhaps most severe in polygamous animals, and the males of such species are the most often equipped with special weapons.
quote: The war is, perhaps, severest between the males of polygamous animals, and these seem oftenest provided with special weapons.
scope: animals with male-male competition for mates, especially mammals and birds
measurable_quantities: mating system (degree of polygyny)
male weapon size or presence
sexual size dimorphism
intensity of male-male combat
candidate_data: Comparative mating-system and morphology data such as PanTHERIA, AVONET and published sexual-dimorphism compilations, analysed on phylogenies from BirdTree or VertLife.

section: Sexual Selection
label: Female choice over many generations can produce male ornaments
claim: Female birds, by choosing the most melodious or beautiful males over thousands of generations, can produce a marked change in male song or plumage.
quote: I can see no good reason to doubt that female birds, by selecting, during thousands of generations, the most melodious or beautiful males, according to their standard of beauty, might produce a marked effect.
scope: birds, especially species with male display
measurable_quantities: female preference for male song or plumage traits
mating success versus ornament expression
ornament evolution across lineages
candidate_data: Mate-choice experiments and field mating-success studies in birds, together with plumage and song comparative datasets analysed on BirdTree phylogenies.

section: Sexual Selection
label: Sex differences in species with shared habits are mainly sexually selected
claim: When males and females of a species share the same general habits of life but differ in structure, colour or ornament, those differences were mainly caused by sexual selection, although not all such differences are.
quote: Thus it is, as I believe, that when the males and females of any animal have the same general habits of life, but differ in structure, colour, or ornament, such differences have been mainly caused by sexual selection
scope: sexually dimorphic animals
measurable_quantities: degree of sexual dimorphism
measures of sexual selection intensity (mating system, variance in male mating success)
ecological differences between sexes
candidate_data: Comparative sexual-dimorphism and mating-system data (e.g. AVONET, PanTHERIA, published bird plumage dichromatism scores) analysed on phylogenies.

section: Natural Selection: its power compared with man’s selection, its power on characters of trifling importance, its power at all ages and on both sexes
label: Flowers and their insect visitors become mutually adapted
claim: A flower and a bee can slowly become modified and adapted to each other, at the same time or one after the other, by the continued preservation of individuals with mutually favourable slight differences in structure.
quote: Thus I can understand how a flower and a bee might slowly become, either simultaneously or one after the other, modified and adapted in the most perfect manner to each other, by the continued preservation of individuals presenting mutual and slightly favourable deviations of structure.
scope: flowering plants and their insect pollinators
measurable_quantities: corolla tube length
pollinator proboscis length
trait matching across plant-pollinator pairs
pollination success versus trait match
candidate_data: Plant-pollinator interaction networks (Web of Life, GloBI) with floral and pollinator trait data, and published studies on correlated tube and tongue lengths.

section: Natural Selection: its power compared with man’s selection, its power on characters of trifling importance, its power at all ages and on both sexes
label: Natural selection works only by accumulating very small modifications
claim: Natural selection acts only by preserving and accumulating very small inherited modifications, each profitable to its bearer, and so excludes continued creation of new organisms or large sudden changes of structure.
quote: Natural selection can act only by the preservation and accumulation of infinitesimally small inherited modifications, each profitable to the preserved being
scope: all organisms
measurable_quantities: distribution of effect sizes of adaptive changes
rates of morphological change between successive generations or fossil samples
candidate_data: Experimental-evolution datasets (e.g. LTEE) and fine-scale fossil sequences in the Paleobiology Database that record morphological change over time.

section: On the generality of intercrosses between individuals of the same species
label: Crossing increases vigour; close interbreeding decreases it
claim: In animals and plants, crosses between different varieties or between different strains of the same variety give vigour and fertility to the offspring, while close interbreeding reduces vigour and fertility.
quote: a cross between different varieties, or between individuals of the same variety but of another strain, gives vigour and fertility to the offspring; and on the other hand, that _close_ interbreeding diminishes vigour and fertility
scope: animals and plants, wild and domestic
measurable_quantities: offspring survival and fertility from outcrosses versus inbred matings
inbreeding depression
heterosis
candidate_data: Meta-analyses of inbreeding depression and heterosis in wild and domestic populations, and pedigreed long-term wild-population and livestock breeding records.

section: On the generality of intercrosses between individuals of the same species
label: No organism self-fertilises indefinitely; occasional crosses are needed
claim: It is a general law of nature that no organism fertilises itself for an unlimited number of generations; an occasional cross with another individual, perhaps at long intervals, is indispensable, even in hermaphrodites.
quote: it is a general law of nature (utterly ignorant though we be of the meaning of the law) that no organic being self-fertilises itself for an eternity of generations; but that a cross with another individual is occasionally—perhaps at very long intervals—indispensable.
scope: all plants and animals, especially hermaphrodites
measurable_quantities: outcrossing rate
persistence and diversification rate of selfing or asexual lineages
longevity of exclusively selfing lineages
candidate_data: Plant mating-system compilations (outcrossing-rate databases in the literature), phylogenetic studies of selfing and asexual lineage age using TimeTree or Open Tree of Life.

section: On the generality of intercrosses between individuals of the same species
label: Trees more often have separate sexes than other plants
claim: Trees, across all plant orders, have separate male and female flowers more often than other plants do, which helps pollen move between trees (though Hooker reported the rule fails in Australia).
quote: That trees belonging to all Orders have their sexes more often separated than other plants, I find to be the case in this country
scope: flowering plants, comparing trees with non-woody plants
measurable_quantities: frequency of dioecy and monoecy in trees versus herbs
growth form
candidate_data: Plant sexual-system and growth-form data from the Tree of Sex database, TRY, and regional floras, analysed on Open Tree of Life phylogenies.

section: Circumstances favourable and unfavourable to Natural Selection, namely, intercrossing, isolation, number of individuals
label: Large populations favour natural selection by supplying more variations
claim: A large number of individuals favours natural selection because it gives a better chance for profitable variations to arise within a given period, compensating for lower variability in each individual.
quote: A large number of individuals, by giving a better chance for the appearance within any given period of profitable variations, will compensate for a lesser amount of variability in each individual, and is, I believe, an extremely important element of success.
scope: all species undergoing natural selection
measurable_quantities: population size
rate of adaptation
rate of appearance of beneficial variants
candidate_data: Experimental-evolution studies that manipulate population size (e.g. microbial evolution datasets deposited in Dryad) and comparative studies of adaptation rate versus population size.

section: Circumstances favourable and unfavourable to Natural Selection, namely, intercrossing, isolation, number of individuals
label: Large areas produce more, faster-forming and wider-spreading new species
claim: Although small isolated areas can favour new species, modification is generally faster on large areas, and forms produced there, having beaten many competitors, spread most widely and give rise to the most new varieties and species.
quote: Finally, I conclude that, although small isolated areas probably have been in some respects highly favourable for the production of new species, yet that the course of modification will generally have been more rapid on large areas; and what is more important, that the new forms produced on large areas, which already have been victorious over many competitors, will be those that will spread most widely
scope: terrestrial species in continents versus islands and small regions
measurable_quantities: speciation or diversification rate versus area
range size and spread of lineages originating in large versus small areas
candidate_data: Dated phylogenies (TimeTree, BirdTree) combined with biogeographic range data (GBIF, IUCN range maps) to estimate diversification rates by region area.

section: Circumstances favourable and unfavourable to Natural Selection, namely, intercrossing, isolation, number of individuals
label: Freshwater biotas evolve and go extinct more slowly, keeping relict forms
claim: Because all freshwater basins together form a small area, competition among freshwater organisms has been less severe, so new forms have arisen more slowly and old forms have been exterminated more slowly there, which is why fresh water holds ancient and anomalous forms.
quote: All fresh-water basins, taken together, make a small area compared with that of the sea or of the land; and, consequently, the competition between fresh-water productions will have been less severe than elsewhere; new forms will have been more slowly formed, and old forms more slowly exterminated.
scope: freshwater organisms, compared with marine and terrestrial ones
measurable_quantities: origination and extinction rates of freshwater versus marine or terrestrial lineages
frequency of relict (living-fossil) lineages by habitat
candidate_data: Paleobiology Database origination and extinction rates by environment, and dated fish phylogenies (e.g. Fish Tree of Life) for diversification by habitat.

section: Slow action
label: Natural selection acts slowly, intermittently and on few species at a time
claim: Natural selection always acts very slowly, often only at long intervals of time, and generally on only a very few of the inhabitants of a region at the same time.
quote: On the other hand, I do believe that natural selection will always act very slowly, often only at long intervals of time, and generally on only a very few of the inhabitants of the same region at the same time.
scope: all organisms within a region over geological time
measurable_quantities: rates of morphological change in fossil lineages
proportion of lineages changing in a given interval
evolutionary stasis versus change in fossil series
candidate_data: Fossil time series and occurrence data in the Paleobiology Database and Neotoma, and compilations of evolutionary rates across timescales.

section: Extinction caused by Natural Selection
label: Favoured forms make less favoured forms rare, and rarity precedes extinction
claim: Because every area is already fully stocked, as a favoured form increases in number the less favoured forms decrease and become rare, and rarity precedes extinction.
quote: it follows that as each selected and favoured form increases in number, so will the less favoured forms decrease and become rare. Rarity, as geology tells us, is the precursor to extinction.
scope: species in fully occupied areas, over ecological and geological time
measurable_quantities: abundance or occupancy decline before extinction
abundance trends of competing species
extinction risk versus rarity
candidate_data: Paleobiology Database occupancy trajectories before extinction, IUCN Red List assessments, and the Living Planet Index abundance trends.

section: Extinction caused by Natural Selection
label: New forms press hardest on and tend to exterminate their nearest relatives
claim: Because the most closely related forms compete most severely, each new variety or species, while forming, presses hardest on its nearest relatives and tends to exterminate them.
quote: Consequently, each new variety or species, during the progress of its formation, will generally press hardest on its nearest kindred, and tend to exterminate them.
scope: varieties and species, wild and domesticated
measurable_quantities: extinction of a lineage in relation to origination of close relatives
phylogenetic clustering of extinctions
replacement of older breeds or varieties by newer ones
candidate_data: Paleobiology Database origination and extinction data analysed for clade replacement, dated phylogenies (TimeTree), and historical records of livestock breed replacement such as FAO DAD-IS.

section: Divergence of Character, related to the diversity of inhabitants of any small area, and to naturalisation
label: Divergence of character maximises the life an area supports
claim: The greatest amount of life can be supported in an area by great diversification of structure among its inhabitants.
quote: The truth of the principle, that the greatest amount of life can be supported by great diversification of structure, is seen under many natural circumstances.
scope: local communities of plants and animals
measurable_quantities: species or genus richness per unit area
biomass or individual density per unit area
candidate_data: Plot-level biodiversity-productivity experiments (e.g. Cedar Creek BigBio, Jena Experiment); sPlot vegetation plots

section: Divergence of Character, related to the diversity of inhabitants of any small area, and to naturalisation
label: The closest-competing neighbours tend to belong to different genera and orders
claim: Where organisms compete most closely, as on a small patch of ground, the advantages of diversification mean that the coexisting inhabitants generally belong to different genera and orders.
quote: where they come into the closest competition with each other, the advantages of diversification of structure, with the accompanying differences of habit and constitution, determine that the inhabitants, which thus jostle each other most closely, shall, as a general rule, belong to what we call different genera and orders.
scope: small-area communities, e.g. turf plots, islets, small ponds
measurable_quantities: genera-to-species and orders-to-species ratios in small plots versus regional pools
phylogenetic dispersion of local communities
candidate_data: Vegetation plot databases (sPlot, BIEN plots) with phylogenies from Open Tree of Life to compute phylogenetic over- or under-dispersion.

section: Divergence of Character, related to the diversity of inhabitants of any small area, and to naturalisation
label: Naturalised floras add proportionally more new genera than new species
claim: Floras gain far more new genera than new species from naturalised plants, relative to the native numbers of genera and species, so naturalised plants tend to differ from the natives at the genus level.
quote: floras gain by naturalisation, proportionally with the number of the native genera and species, far more in new genera than in new species.
scope: naturalised plants in regional floras
measurable_quantities: proportion of naturalised species in genera absent from the native flora
species-to-genus ratio of naturalised versus native floras
phylogenetic distance of naturalised species to natives
candidate_data: GloNAF naturalised-flora checklists compared with native floras, with phylogenetic distances from Open Tree of Life.

section: Action of Natural Selection, through Divergence of Character and Extinction, on the descendants from a common parent
label: Intermediate forms and parent species tend to go extinct
claim: In a fully stocked country, improved descendants of a species tend to supplant their predecessors, so the intermediate forms between earlier and later states, and the original parent species itself, generally tend to become extinct.
quote: Hence all the intermediate forms between the earlier and later states, that is between the less and more improved state of a species, as well as the original parent-species itself, will generally tend to become extinct.
scope: lineages of species descended from a common parent
measurable_quantities: persistence of ancestral morphotypes alongside descendants
frequency of budding versus anagenetic replacement in fossil lineages
survival of intermediate morphologies
candidate_data: Paleobiology Database occurrence data and published ancestor-descendant fossil series (e.g. planktonic foraminifera lineage data).

section: Action of Natural Selection, through Divergence of Character and Extinction, on the descendants from a common parent
label: Extinct species are often intermediate between living groups
claim: Extinct species, though generally in the same orders, families or genera as living ones, are often somewhat intermediate in character between existing groups, because they lived when the branching lines of descent had diverged less.
quote: the diagram throws light on the affinities of extinct beings, which, though generally belonging to the same orders, or families, or genera, with those now living, yet are often, in some degree, intermediate in character between existing groups
scope: fossil and living species of all groups
measurable_quantities: morphological position of fossil taxa relative to living groups
phylogenetic placement of fossils (stem versus crown)
disparity between groups through time
candidate_data: Paleobiology Database taxonomy, morphological character matrices in MorphoBank, and phylogenies including fossils in Open Tree of Life.

section: Summary
label: Differences between varieties grow into differences between species and genera
claim: Through natural selection and divergence of character, the small differences between varieties of a species steadily increase until they equal the larger differences between species of the same genus, or even between genera.
quote: Thus the small differences distinguishing varieties of the same species, will steadily tend to increase till they come to equal the greater differences between species of the same genus, or even of distinct genera.
scope: varieties, species and genera of all organisms
measurable_quantities: phenotypic divergence versus time since divergence
divergence of within-species varieties compared with between-species differences
candidate_data: Dated phylogenies (TimeTree) combined with trait data (AVONET, TRY) to relate trait divergence to divergence time, and fossil series in the Paleobiology Database.

section: Explains the Grouping of all organic beings
label: Descent with divergence and extinction explains nested classification
claim: The arrangement of all organisms in groups nested within groups (varieties within species, species within genera, and so on up to classes) is explained by inheritance and natural selection with its accompanying extinction and divergence of character, not by independent creation.
quote: On the view that each species has been independently created, I can see no explanation of this great fact in the classification of all organic beings; but, to the best of my judgment, it is explained through inheritance and the complex action of natural selection, entailing extinction and divergence of character, as we have seen illustrated in the diagram.
scope: all animals and plants, living and extinct
measurable_quantities: degree of hierarchical (tree-like) structure in character data
congruence between independent character sets
candidate_data: Open Tree of Life synthetic tree, GenBank sequence data, and MorphoBank morphological matrices to test hierarchical structure and congruence.

section: Summary
label: Very few species of past periods have living descendants
claim: Like a tree in which only a few early twigs grew into surviving branches, very few of the species that lived in long-past geological periods now have living modified descendants, and many whole orders, families and genera have died out entirely.
quote: Of the many twigs which flourished when the tree was a mere bush, only two or three, now grown into great branches, yet survive and bear all the other branches; so with the species which lived during long-past geological periods, very few now have living and modified descendants.
scope: all lineages over geological time
measurable_quantities: fraction of species or clades in a past interval with living descendants
clade extinction rates
shape of phylogenies including fossils
candidate_data: Paleobiology Database occurrence and range data, combined with time-calibrated phylogenies from TimeTree and Open Tree of Life.
